title: Given a `List<Employee>` where the `city` field can be null, sort by city alphabetically but push all employees with a null city to the end, using `Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder())`.
shortTitle: Sort employees with nulls-last for a nullable field using Comparator.nullsLast

s1_definition.profdef: `Comparator.nullsLast(wrapped)` returns a null-friendly comparator that treats `null` as greater than any non-null value, so nulls sort to the end, and delegates all non-null comparisons to the wrapped comparator. Combined with `Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))` it safely sorts on a nullable key without throwing `NullPointerException`.
s1_definition.analogy: Some employees at the National Bank of India have not filled in their city yet, so that field is blank (null). Priya wants the list sorted by city A to Z, but everyone with a missing city should sit at the bottom rather than crash the sort. `nullsLast` says "treat a missing value as 'comes last'".
s1_definition.oneliner: `nullsLast(naturalOrder())` sorts real values normally and pushes nulls to the end instead of crashing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Comparator.nullsLast(wrapped)` returns a null-friendly comparator that treats `null` as greater than any non-null value, so nulls sort to the end, and delegates all non-null comparisons to the wrapped comparator. Combined with `Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))` it safely sorts on a nullable key without throwing `NullPointerException`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Some employees at the National Bank of India have not filled in their city yet, so that field is blank (null). Priya wants the list sorted by city A to Z, but everyone with a missing city should sit at the bottom rather than crash the sort. `nullsLast` says "treat a missing value as 'comes last'".

**One line to remember:** `nullsLast(naturalOrder())` sorts real values normally and pushes nulls to the end instead of crashing.

sections.s2_technical:
A plain `Comparator.comparing(Employee::getCity)` throws a `NullPointerException` the moment it tries to compare a null city, because it calls `compareTo` on null. `Comparator.nullsLast` fixes this by wrapping a comparator and intercepting nulls: if either value is null it decides the order directly (null is "bigger", so it goes last) and only calls the wrapped comparator when both values are non-null.

There are two common ways to apply it to a field. The most explicit is `Comparator.comparing(Employee::getCity, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))` — this extracts the city and compares it with a null-safe natural-order comparator. The sibling method `Comparator.nullsFirst` does the opposite, sending nulls to the top.

A senior point: `nullsLast` protects against a null field value, but if the Employee object itself could be null you would also guard the stream, for instance by filtering `Objects::nonNull` first. For a stable, predictable report I often add a `thenComparing(Employee::getName)` so employees in the same city, including the null-city group, are ordered by name.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's employee records are partially migrated, so some staff have no city recorded yet. A direct city sort throws a NullPointerException and the whole report fails. This is exactly the problem `nullsLast` solves — it treats a missing city as "sort last" instead of crashing.

Problem 2 — Management still wants the incomplete records visible, just at the bottom, and wants same-city employees ordered by name. This is exactly how `nullsLast(naturalOrder())` plus a name tie-breaker works.

The code defines `Employee` with a nullable city, a `DirectoryService` with `sortByCityNullsLast`, and a runnable demo including two null-city employees.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh "Mumbai", Priya null, Amit "Bengaluru", Sneha null, Vikram "Delhi".

Step 1: The null-safe city comparator compares non-null cities alphabetically: Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai.

Step 2: Both null-city employees, Priya and Sneha, are treated as "greater" than any city, so they move to the end.

Step 3: Within the null-city group the name tie-breaker orders Priya before Sneha.

Step 4: `toList()` returns the new list; no NullPointerException is thrown and the input is unchanged.

```
INFO: Directory (city A-Z, missing city last):
INFO:   Amit      | Bengaluru
INFO:   Vikram    | Delhi
INFO:   Rajesh    | Mumbai
INFO:   Priya     | <none>
INFO:   Sneha     | <none>
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh/Mumbai, Priya/null, Amit/Bengaluru, Sneha/null, Vikram/Delhi]
    │
    ▼
  sorted( comparing(city, nullsLast(naturalOrder())).thenComparing(name) )
    │
    ├─ non-null cities A→Z → Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai
    ├─ nulls treated as "greatest" → pushed to end
    └─ tie within null group → name A→Z → Priya, Sneha
    ▼
  toList() → NEW list (NO NullPointerException)
    ▼
  Output: Amit/Bengaluru, Vikram/Delhi, Rajesh/Mumbai, Priya/null, Sneha/null
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I sort on a field that can be null I never use a plain comparator, because the moment it compares a null it throws a NullPointerException and the whole report fails. Instead I wrap the key comparator with `Comparator.nullsLast`, writing `Comparator.comparing(Employee::getCity, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))`. That treats null as greater than any real value, so employees with a missing city sort to the end while every non-null city is ordered alphabetically, and nothing crashes.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this came straight out of a half-finished data migration where some employee records had no city yet. The directory report needed those incomplete records visible but parked at the bottom, and `nullsLast` did exactly that. I also added a name tie-breaker so same-city employees, including the whole null-city group, were ordered predictably.

The senior points I raise are that `nullsFirst` is the mirror image if you want nulls at the top, that `nullsLast` guards a null field value but not a null Employee object, so if the object itself could be null I would filter with `Objects::nonNull` first, and that the sort still returns a fresh list without mutating the source.

---

keyPoints: reversed() for descending, thenComparing() for secondary sort
sorted() is stateful — buffers all elements before passing downstream
